items.title: Seeds of All Three Realms, Wherever One Is Born

items.zh: 復次，此一切種子識，若般涅槃法者，一切種子皆悉具足。不般涅槃法者，便闕三種菩提種子。
items.en: Further, as for this all-seeds consciousness: in one who has the nature to attain final nirvāṇa, all seeds are fully present. In one who does not have this nature, the seeds of the three kinds of awakening are lacking.

items.zh: 隨所生處，自體之中，餘體種子皆悉隨逐。是故欲界自體中，亦有色、無色界一切種子。如是色界自體中，亦有欲、無色界一切種子。無色界自體中，亦有欲、色界一切種子。
items.en: Wherever one is born, within that very existence, the seeds belonging to the other realms of existence all continue to follow along. Hence, within an existence in the desire realm, all the seeds of the form and formless realms are also present. Likewise, within an existence in the form realm, all the seeds of the desire and formless realms are also present. And within an existence in the formless realm, all the seeds of the desire and form realms are also present.

items.title: The Embryo Grows Towards Complete Support

items.zh: 又羯羅藍漸增長時，名之與色平等增長，俱漸廣大。如是增長，乃至依止圓滿應知。
items.en: Further, as the kalala gradually grows, name (the mental aggregates) grows evenly together with form (the kalala's matter), both gradually expanding. This growth continues until what is called complete support is reached.

items.title: How the Four Elements Build the Body

items.zh: 此中由地界故，依止造色漸漸增廣。由水界故，攝持不散。由火界故，成熟堅鞕。由無潤故，由風界故，分別肢節各安其所。
items.en: Here, through the earth element, the derived matter dependent on it gradually grows and expands. Through the water element, it is held together and does not disperse. Through the fire element, it ripens into firmness. And, once moisture no longer holds them fused, through the wind element, the limbs and joints are separated out, each set in its own proper place.

items.zh: 又一切種子識，於生自體雖有淨不淨業因，然唯樂著戲論為最勝因。於生族姓、色力、壽量、資具等果，即淨不淨業為最勝因。
items.en: Further, in the arising of a being's own existence — the [six] sense-faculties themselves — although pure and impure karma serve as a cause, it is delight in elaboration alone that is the dominant cause. But in the fruits of one's lineage, physical beauty and strength, lifespan, and material resources, it is pure and impure karma that is the dominant cause.

items.zh: 又諸凡夫，於自體上計我、我所，及起我慢。一切聖者，觀唯是苦。
又處胎分中，有自性受，不苦不樂，依識增長。唯此性受，異熟所攝。餘一切受，或異熟所生，或境界緣生。又苦受、樂受，或於一時從緣現起，或時不起。
items.en: Further, within the womb, there is an intrinsic feeling — neither painful nor pleasant — that grows in step with consciousness. Only this intrinsic feeling belongs strictly to the ripened result. All other feeling arises either from the ripened result or from present sensory conditions. Painful and pleasant feeling, moreover, sometimes arise from such conditions, and sometimes do not arise at all.

items.title: How Seeds Keep Producing Results, Life After Life

items.zh: 又種子體，無始時來相續不絕。性雖無始有之，然由淨不淨業差別熏發，望數數取異熟果，說彼為新。若果已生，說此種子為已受果。由此道理，生死流轉相續不絕，乃至未般涅槃。
items.en: Further, the continuum of seeds has continued without break since beginningless time. Though its nature has existed from the beginning, because it is activated again and again, in different ways, by pure and impure karma, and repeatedly gives rise to a ripened result, it is spoken of, each time, as though newly arisen. Once a result has arisen, that seed is said to have already yielded its result. Through this principle, the cycle of birth and death continues without interruption, until final nirvāṇa is attained.

items.zh: 又諸種子未與果者，或順生受，或順後受。雖經百千劫，從自種子一切自體復圓滿生。雖餘果生要由自種，若至壽量盡邊，爾時此種名已受果。所餘自體種子未與果故，不名已受果。
items.en: Further, of seeds that have not yet yielded their result, some yield it in the very next life, others only in some later life. Even after hundreds of thousands of eons, once conditions ripen, a complete new existence still arises from that very seed. Though every new existence depends on its own seed, it is only when the present lifespan reaches its end that this seed is said to have already yielded its result; other seeds belonging to this same existence, not yet having yielded a result, are not said to have already yielded one.

items.zh: 又諸種子，即於此身中應受異熟，緣差不受。順不定受攝故。然此種子亦唯住此位。
items.en: Further, there are seeds that ought to produce a ripened result within this very body, but which, for lack of the right conditions, do not do so — these belong to the class of uncertain karma. Such a seed, nonetheless, simply continues to reside within the ālayavijñāna.

items.zh: 是故一一自體中，皆有一切自體種子。若於一處有染欲，即說一切處有染欲。若於一處得離欲，即說於一切處得離欲。
items.en: Therefore, within each and every existence, the seeds of every possible existence are all present. If, in one place, defiled craving is present, it is said that defiled craving is present in every place. And if, in one place, freedom from craving is attained, it is said that freedom from craving is attained in every place.

items.zh: 又於諸自體中所有種子，若煩惱品所攝，名為麁重，亦名隨眠。若異熟品所攝，及餘無記品所攝，唯名麁重，不名隨眠。若信等善法品所攝種子，不名麁重，亦非隨眠。
items.en: Further, among all the seeds present within any existence: those belonging to the class of afflictions are called both "coarse burden" and "latent tendency." Those belonging to the class of ripened results, and other indeterminate classes, are called only "coarse burden," not "latent tendency." And those belonging to the class of wholesome factors such as faith are called neither "coarse burden" nor "latent tendency."

items.zh: 何以故？由此法生時，所依自體唯有堪能，非不堪能。

items.title: Why Even a Neutral Existence Counts as Suffering

items.zh: 是故一切所依自體，麁重所隨故，麁重所生故，麁重自性故，諸佛如來安立為苦，所謂由行苦故。
items.en: Therefore, every underlying existence — followed by coarse burden, produced by coarse burden, and having coarse burden as its very nature — is established by the Buddhas as suffering: this is what is meant by suffering through the nature of conditioned formations.

items.zh: 又諸種子，乃有多種差別之名。所謂名界、名種姓，名自性，名因，名薩迦耶，名戲論，名阿賴耶，名取，名苦，名薩迦耶見所依止處，名我慢所依止處。如是等類，差別應知。
items.en: Further, these seeds go by many different names: realm, lineage, own-nature, cause, personal existence, elaboration, the storehouse, appropriation, suffering, the basis of the view of a personal existence, and the basis of conceit. Distinctions of this kind should be understood.

items.title: Two Paths to Transforming the Basis

items.zh: 又般涅槃時，已得轉依諸淨行者，轉捨一切染污法種子所依。於一切善、無記法種子，轉令緣闕，轉得內緣自在。
items.en: Further, at the time of final nirvāṇa, those pure practitioners who have attained the transformation of the basis relinquish the basis for all seeds of defiled dharmas. As for the seeds of wholesome and indeterminate dharmas: in one case, the conditions for their future ripening are made to fail; in the other, one attains mastery over these very seeds from within.

items.zh: 又於胎中，經三十八七日，此之胎藏，一切支分皆悉具足。從此已後、復經四日方乃出生。如薄伽梵於入胎經廣說。此說極滿足者，或經九月、或復過此。若唯經八月，此名圓滿，非極圓滿。
items.en: Further, within the womb, after thirty-eight weeks, the foetus has all its limbs and parts fully formed. After this, a further four days pass before birth. The Blessed One explained this at length in the Sūtra on Entering the Womb. What is here called utterly complete refers to nine months, or slightly more. If only eight months have passed, this is called complete, but not utterly complete.

blocks.text: Fascicle 2 continues the Mind Stage's account of birth, but before following the embryo further it pauses for a dense passage on **seeds**. This is one of the most important doctrinal passages in the early fascicles: it explains why every existence contains the potential for every other, why even a neutral life counts as suffering, and what happens to the seeds at nirvāṇa. Read it slowly; the embryology resumes at the end.

Two short sentences are untranslated. At 0284b14 the treatise says that ordinary beings take their own existence to be "I" and "mine" and give rise to conceit, while all noble ones see it as nothing but suffering. At 0284c07 it explains why wholesome seeds such as faith are neither "coarse burden" nor "latent tendency": when they arise, the basis is only fit, never unfit.

subs.head: All seeds, wherever one is born

blocks.text: The ālayavijñāna of a being who has the nature to reach nirvāṇa holds all seeds; one who lacks that nature lacks the seeds of the three kinds of awakening (those of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha). Venerable Miào Jìng reassures his listeners: "Anyone who has faith in the Buddha has the seeds of awakening complete … you can set your mind at ease."

Wherever one is born, the seeds of every other realm come along. A human in the desire realm carries the seeds of the form and formless realms. Master Cháng Bǎi draws the practical lesson: meditative absorption is possible for us "because these seeds are certainly in the ālayavijñāna. The question is only whether one puts in the effort."
Both teachers note a subtle wording, echoing Day 3: impure seeds "follow along with" the ālayavijñāna, while pure seeds are only "annexed to" it, like guests, because they differ in nature from it.

Name (the mental aggregates) and form grow together until the body is complete. Each of the four elements does its work: earth makes it grow, water holds it together, fire ripens it into firmness, and wind, once the moisture stops binding everything, separates the limbs into their places. Venerable Miào Jìng's homely gloss: water must stop at the right point, or the fingers would stay stuck together.

A crucial distinction. For the arising of an existence itself, karma helps, but the **dominant cause** is "delight in elaboration", that is, the linguistic seeds (名言種子) laid down by our habit of naming and grasping. For the *quality* of that existence (family, beauty, strength, lifespan, wealth), karma is dominant. Master Cháng Bǎi: karma decides what kind of life one has; the deeper habit of taking things as conceptually real is what produces a life to have at all. Venerable Miào Jìng compares it to wheat: soil, water, and sun help, but without the seed nothing grows.

In the womb there is a neutral **intrinsic feeling** (自性受) that grows with consciousness; it alone strictly belongs to the ripened result, while pleasure and pain come and go. Venerable Miào Jìng: this is the ālayavijñāna's own neutral feeling; even in hell "the ālayavijñāna does not feel pain". The *Pīxún jì*'s image, quoted by Master Cháng Bǎi, is a burning sore: cold on it feels pleasant, hot ash painful, and only apart from both does the sore's own pain show. The point: underneath pleasure and pain, existence itself is a subtle discomfort we rarely notice.

Seeds may ripen in the next life or after "hundreds of thousands of eons", but they do not disappear. Some karma is fixed, some uncertain. Both teachers give the same criterion: an act done deliberately and gladly, without regret, is fixed; an act regretted and repented is no longer certain to ripen in full. Master Cháng Bǎi adds that the same offering made wholeheartedly or carelessly plants seeds of very different weight.

Because every existence contains the seeds of every other, craving present in one place counts as present everywhere, and freedom from craving attained in one place counts as freedom everywhere. Master Cháng Bǎi explains why non-Buddhist meditators who reach the highest formless realm still fall back: they only suppressed craving for the realms below, without uprooting self-love, which is the same in every realm.

items: **Coarse burden** (麁重, *dauṣṭhulya*) is "lack of fitness" of the basis. Venerable Miào Jìng's example: "When I sit, I can't count the breath, I can't contemplate non-self, but daydreaming, that I can do; for that I have fitness."
**Latent tendency** (隨眠, *anuśaya*) is the dormant seed of an affliction, ready to become active.

blocks.text: Afflictive seeds are both; seeds of the ripened result and other neutral seeds are only coarse burden; wholesome seeds are neither.

subs.head: Why even a neutral life is suffering

blocks.text: Because every existence is followed by, produced by, and made of coarse burden, the Buddhas establish it as **suffering of conditioned formations** (行苦, *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), even when no pain is felt. Venerable Miào Jìng quotes the *Abhidharmakośa*: an eyelash on the palm is not felt, but in the eye it hurts. Ordinary people are like the palm; the wise, like the eye.

Seeds are also called realm, lineage, own-nature, cause, personal existence, elaboration, the storehouse (阿賴耶, *ālaya*), appropriation, suffering, the basis of the view of a self, and the basis of conceit. Each name highlights one function; together they show how much the single idea of "seed" carries.

subs.head: Two ways of transforming the basis

blocks.text: At final nirvāṇa, those who have attained the **transformation of the basis** abandon all defiled seeds. For the wholesome and neutral seeds there are two outcomes: the śrāvaka simply lets them lose the conditions to ripen, while bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above gain "mastery over them from within" and use them to manifest bodies for the benefit of beings. Venerable Miào Jìng stresses that concentration alone cannot remove defiled seeds; only the wisdom of emptiness can.
After thirty-eight weeks the body is complete; four days later comes birth, about nine months in all. Tomorrow the treatise goes back and describes the eight weekly stages in detail.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what is lacking in the all-seeds consciousness of one who does not have the nature to attain final nirvāṇa?
options: the seeds of the desire realm
all contaminated seeds
the ālayavijñāna itself
the seeds of the three kinds of awakening
quiz.why: "In one who has the nature to attain final nirvāṇa, all seeds are fully present. In one who does not have this nature, the seeds of the three kinds of awakening are lacking." The three are the awakening of the śrāvaka, of the pratyekabuddha, and great awakening (a Buddha's) — both teachers and the *Pixunji* agree. B is the reverse: such beings, as Master Cháng Bǎi says, have only contaminated seeds. Venerable Miào Jìng reassures his listeners: "Anyone who has faith in the Buddha has the seeds of awakening complete … you can set your mind at ease."

quiz.q: The treatise says that within a desire-realm existence, all the seeds of the form and formless realms are also present. What conclusion do both teachers draw?
options: someone born in the desire realm can still attain the absorptions of the form and formless realms through effort — the seeds were never absent, only waiting on conditions
desire-realm beings are automatically reborn in the form realm
form- and formless-realm seeds decay in the desire realm
seeds can only function in the realm one is born into
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Even though one is born in the desire realm, if one works hard one will surely attain meditative absorption, because these seeds are certainly in the ālayavijñāna. The question is only whether one puts in the effort." Venerable Miào Jìng says the same: to make them active "you must make further effort, you must practise further." B is wrong about "automatically" — the seeds become active only when strengthened by practice. Conversely, beings born even in the realm of neither perception nor non-perception fall back after eighty thousand eons, because their desire-realm seeds remain.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what is the dominant cause in the arising of a being's own existence — and what is the dominant cause of lineage, beauty and strength, lifespan, and resources?
options: for one's existence itself, delight in elaboration (linguistic seeds) is dominant; for lineage, beauty, lifespan, and resources, pure and impure karma is dominant
pure and impure karma is dominant in both
the parents' fluids are dominant for one's existence
delight in elaboration is dominant for lineage and the rest
quiz.why: "In the arising of a being's own existence … although pure and impure karma serve as a cause, it is delight in elaboration alone that is the dominant cause. But in the fruits of one's lineage, physical beauty and strength, lifespan, and material resources, it is pure and impure karma that is the dominant cause." Venerable Miào Jìng compares it to wheat: water, soil, sunlight, and wind all help, but without the seed nothing grows — linguistic seeds directly produce the result. Master Cháng Bǎi: karma decides what kind of life one has; the deeper habit of taking things as conceptually real is what produces a life to have in the first place.

quiz.q: What kind of feeling is the "intrinsic feeling" in the womb, according to the treatise?
options: neither painful nor pleasant, growing in step with consciousness; only this intrinsic feeling belongs strictly to the ripened result
intense painful feeling
pleasant feeling that arises only when the mother eats
pain and pleasure that come and go
quiz.why: "There is an intrinsic feeling — neither painful nor pleasant — that grows in step with consciousness. Only this intrinsic feeling belongs strictly to the ripened result." C and D describe "all other feeling," which arises from the ripened result or from present sensory conditions, and "sometimes arise[s] … and sometimes do[es] not arise at all." Master Cháng Bǎi: as long as the foetus lives, the neutral feeling is always present, while pain and pleasure are not. Venerable Miào Jìng: the intrinsic feeling is really the ālayavijñāna's own neutral feeling, morally indeterminate.

quiz.q: What criterion do both teachers use to distinguish fixed karma from uncertain karma?
options: by the size of the act — small acts are always uncertain
by whether the act was done deliberately and whether one regrets it: done on purpose and gladly, without regret, it is fixed; regretted and repented, its result is no longer certain
by the realm in which it is done
by whether others know about it
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Fully aware — 'I want to do this' … and once done, still happy about it: that is fixed karma"; "if I regret it afterwards and repent, then it is no longer certain." Master Cháng Bǎi: "If one regrets it afterwards, it is called uncertain karma," adding that repentance works — heavy karma can ripen lightly. The *Pixunji* defines uncertain karma as light karma done intentionally. Master Cháng Bǎi also notes that the same offering made wholeheartedly or carelessly plants seeds of very different weight.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what are the seeds belonging to the class of ripened results and other indeterminate classes called?
options: both "coarse burden" and "latent tendency"
neither "coarse burden" nor "latent tendency"
only "coarse burden," not "latent tendency"
only "latent tendency," not "coarse burden"
quiz.why: The treatise sorts three classes: afflictive seeds are "both 'coarse burden' and 'latent tendency'" (A); seeds of the ripened and other indeterminate classes are "only 'coarse burden,' not 'latent tendency'" (C); wholesome seeds such as faith are "neither" (B). The *Pixunji*: the ripened class is called coarse burden because it lacks fitness, but not latent tendency because it does not generate affliction. D does not appear in the text.

quiz.q: The treatise says the Buddhas establish "every underlying existence" as suffering. Which suffering, and why?
options: the suffering of pain, because the body often falls ill
the suffering of change, because pleasure vanishes
the suffering of not getting what one wants
the suffering of conditioned formations — because it is followed by coarse burden, produced by coarse burden, and has coarse burden as its very nature
quiz.why: "Therefore, every underlying existence — followed by coarse burden, produced by coarse burden, and having coarse burden as its very nature — is established by the Buddhas as suffering: this is what is meant by suffering through the nature of conditioned formations." Master Cháng Bǎi: even an existence untouched at this moment by active affliction still counts as suffering, which is why the classical shorthand for suffering is "the five aggregates of clinging." Venerable Miào Jìng: in neutral moments ordinary people feel their bodies are fine, yet right up to the peak of existence it is all the suffering of formations.
